meta.drug: extended-release niacin (Niaspan) 1500-2000 mg/day added to simvastatin (+/- ezetimibe)
meta.sponsor: NHLBI (NIH) with Abbott Laboratories support; registry lead sponsor Axio Research LLC (coordinating center)
meta.mechanism: Nicotinic acid; agonist of HCAR2 (GPR109A / HM74A), which mediates adipocyte anti-lipolysis and PGD2-driven flushing. Target attribution is ambiguous: lipid effects (HDL-C up, TG/LDL-C/apoB/Lp(a) down) appear to be largely HCAR2-independent (proposed hepatic DGAT2 inhibition, reduced VLDL/apoB and apo(a) production, reduced HDL holoparticle uptake); Lauring et al. 2012 showed lipid efficacy persists in GPR109A-knockout mice and full GPR109A agonists failed to change lipids in humans. The trial tested the 'raise HDL-C / treat atherogenic dyslipidemia' hypothesis rather than a single molecular target.
meta.indication: secondary prevention in established atherosclerotic CVD with atherogenic dyslipidemia (low HDL-C, elevated TG) on intensive statin therapy with LDL-C 40-80 mg/dL

n_randomized.quote: A total of 3414 patients were randomly assigned to receive niacin (1718) or placebo (1696).

median_followup.quote: for an average of 36 months follow-up, maximum 66 months
median_followup.note: Mean, not median (median NOT FOUND). NEJM abstract (S1): 'The trial was stopped after a mean follow-up period of 3 years owing to a lack of efficacy.' NHLBI FAQ at stopping (S5): 'The actual average follow-up is 32 months.' Planned mean follow-up was 4.6 years (S3) / 4.1 years (S4).

primary_endpoint.value: Time to first of CHD death, nonfatal MI, ischemic stroke, hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome, or symptom-driven coronary or cerebral revascularization
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary end point was the first event of the composite of death from coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, hospitalization for an acute coronary syndrome, or symptom-driven coronary or cerebral revascularization.
primary_endpoint.note: Endpoint was EXPANDED by protocol amendment 5 (April 2010) because of a lower-than-expected event rate; original endpoint was CHD death, nonfatal MI, ischemic stroke or high-risk ACS hospitalization (S3).

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Age >=45 with established CVD (CAD, cerebrovascular/carotid disease or PAD) and atherogenic dyslipidemia: HDL-C <=40 mg/dL men / <=50 women, TG 150-400 mg/dL, LDL-C <=180 mg/dL if off statin (adjusted thresholds if on statin)
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Participants were men and women, age 45 years or older with atherogenic dyslipidemia and documented, clinically established atherosclerotic CV disease
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Off-statin lipid criteria (Table 1): 'HDL-C ≤ 40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L) for men or ≤ 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L) for women Triglycerides 150 – 400 mg/dL (1.7 – 4.5 mmol/L)'. All patients then treated with simvastatin 40-80 mg +/- ezetimibe 10 mg to LDL-C 40-80 mg/dL in BOTH arms. Placebo contained 50 mg immediate-release niacin per tablet to preserve blinding (flush).

planned_events.quote: This event-driven trial will have 85% power to show a 25% reduction in primary event frequency after 850 patients have experienced a primary outcome event.
planned_events.note: After endpoint expansion (amendment 5, April 2010). Original design: ~3,300 patients, 99% power for 25% reduction assuming 0.089 placebo hazard rate.

assumed_rrr.quote: This event-driven trial will have 85% power to show a 25% reduction in primary event frequency after 850 patients have experienced a primary outcome event.
assumed_rrr.note: A 25% relative reduction is large relative to the small achieved between-arm LDL-C/apoB differences.

power.quote: This event-driven trial will have 85% power to show a 25% reduction in primary event frequency

alpha.quote: using an unadjusted one-sided p-value of 0.025
alpha.note: Stated for the ORIGINAL design (3,300 patients, 99% power); alpha for the amended 850-event design not separately stated. Equivalent to two-sided 0.05.

stopped_early.quote: The trial was stopped early because the study hypothesis was answered, namely there was a lack of efficacy.
stopped_early.note: DSMB recommendation at planned interim analysis on 25 April 2011 (S8); stopped 18 months early (S5: 'The study was stopped 18 months early.'). Unexplained ischemic-stroke excess also contributed. FAQ: <1 in 10,000 chance of showing benefit if continued. Fraction of planned events: final adjudicated primary events 556 (282+274) / 850 planned = ~0.65 (computed; event count at the interim look NOT FOUND).

baseline.quote: Among participants on a statin at entry (94%), mean baseline LDL-C was 71 mg/dL (1.84 mmol/L)
baseline.note: Statin-treated participants (94%). NEJM abstract (S1) reports niacin-arm median LDL-C 74 mg/dL at baseline. Very low LDL-C background (intensive statin +/- ezetimibe).
Least-square mean baseline in placebo arm (82.0) and ERN arm (81.8); prior-statin users with paired samples only.

baseline.quote: the median level of Lp(a) (33.8 nmol/L) was elevated as compared to the median Lp(a) level (20 nmol/L) of healthy, predominantly Caucasian adults from Framingham
baseline.location: Results, Baseline Apolipoprotein and Lp(a) Levels

baseline.note: NOT FOUND in accessible sources (NEJM full text paywalled).

biomarker_effects.quote: but the observed mean lipid differences were small (0.12 mmol/L lower LDL-C and 0.13 mmol/L higher HDL-C in the niacin group)
biomarker_effects.note: Secondary citation of AIM-HIGH by HPS2-THRIVE investigators (open full text). S12 (HPS2-THRIVE NEJM discussion): 'increased the HDL cholesterol level by 5 mg per deciliter.' Original AIM-HIGH NEJM figures not read (paywalled).

biomarker_effects.quote: In the niacin group, HDL increased by 25% and triglycerides decreased by 28.6%. In the placebo group, HDL increased by 9.8% and triglycerides decreased by 8.1%.
biomarker_effects.note: change_pct is the computed difference in percent change (25.0 - 9.8 = 15.2 percentage points); secondary source. Within-arm niacin medians from NEJM abstract (S1): 'increased the median HDL cholesterol level from 35 mg per deciliter (0.91 mmol per liter) to 42 mg per deciliter (1.08 mmol per liter)'. Placebo HDL rose because of statin up-titration/IR niacin in placebo tablets.

biomarker_effects.method: not stated in citing source; core lab Northwest Lipid Metabolism and Diabetes Research Laboratories (LDL method — Friedewald vs direct — NOT FOUND)
biomarker_effects.quote: but the observed mean lipid differences were small (0.12 mmol/L lower LDL-C and 0.13 mmol/L higher HDL-C in the niacin group)
biomarker_effects.note: S12: 'reduced the LDL cholesterol level by only 5 mg per deciliter'. Small difference partly because simvastatin/ezetimibe were titrated to LDL-C 40-80 mg/dL in both arms (more intensification in placebo arm). NEJM abstract within-niacin-arm median LDL 74 -> 62 mg/dL at 2 years (not placebo-adjusted).

biomarker_effects.quote: In the niacin group, HDL increased by 25% and triglycerides decreased by 28.6%. In the placebo group, HDL increased by 9.8% and triglycerides decreased by 8.1%.
biomarker_effects.note: Computed difference (-28.6 - (-8.1) = -20.5 points); secondary source. NEJM abstract (S1) within-niacin-arm median TG 164 -> 122 mg/dL at 2 years.

biomarker_effects.quote: In the ERN group and the placebo group, apoB decreased by 13% and 3%, apoA-1 increased by 7% and 2% and the apoB/apoA-1 ratio decreased by 19% and 7%, respectively
biomarker_effects.location: Results; Table 1 (Diff. in % Chg vs placebo −10.7, p<0.001)
biomarker_effects.note: Least-square mean difference in % change; prior-statin users (n=1424 ERN, 1443 placebo with paired samples). Absolute: ERN 81.8->71.3 vs placebo 82.0->79.6 mg/dL (~-8 mg/dL net).

biomarker_effects.method: monoclonal antibody-based ELISA (Northwest Lipid lab; isoform-insensitive reference method)
biomarker_effects.quote: An overall decrease of 6% for Lp(a) was also observed in the placebo group; thus the overall least-square mean decrease in Lp(a) due to ERN was 19%.
biomarker_effects.note: ERN arm −21.0% vs placebo −5.9%; mean 80.2->63.4 nmol/L (ERN) vs 78.3->73.7 (placebo).
NOT FOUND (AIM-HIGH NEJM full text paywalled; not in open secondary papers read).

biomarker_effects.quote: both NER/S doses resulted in significant improvements in all three parameters (+21.9%, -31.8%, and -21.0%, respectively, for NER/S 2000/40 mg/day)
biomarker_effects.note: PRE-READOUT lipid study (SEACOAST II, 2008): niacin ER/simvastatin 2000/40 vs simvastatin 80 (active comparator, not placebo); values are within-arm % change for HDL-C, TG, Lp(a). Simvastatin 80 'did not alter HDL-C, triglycerides, or lipoprotein(a)'.

hr.quote: (hazard ratio, 1.02; 95% confidence interval, 0.87 to 1.21; P=0.79 by the log-rank test)
hr.note: Registry S2 also reports HR 1.02 (0.87-1.21), Cox regression adjusted for gender and diabetes.

p.note: Registry (S2) reports p=0.80 from adjusted Cox model.

events_treatment.quote: The primary end point occurred in 282 patients in the niacin group (16.4%)

events_control.quote: and in 274 patients in the placebo group (16.2%)

safety_signals.quote: there were 50 fatal or non-fatal ischemic strokes, 18 (1.06%) in placebo arm versus 32 (1.86%) in ERN arm: age-adjusted hazard ratio, HR 1.78 (95% CI 1.00–3.17, p=0.050)
safety_signals.note: Final adjudicated analysis (2013). Multivariable HR 1.74 (0.97–3.11, p=0.063), not significant. At stopping, NHLBI cited 'an unexplained higher rate of ischemic stroke in the high dose niacin group' as contributing (S5). Interim press coverage cited 28 vs 12 (secondary, cardiobrief; not verified). NEJM (via S10): ischemic stroke as first event 1.6% vs 0.9%.
Reported in 2014 after HPS2-THRIVE flagged infection; 139 vs 98 patients.

safety_signals.quote: The overall observed rate of serious hemorrhagic adverse events was low, with no significant difference between the two groups in the trial (3.4% vs. 2.9%, P = 0.36)
safety_signals.note: Bleeding of any severity 10.1% vs 8.1%, P=0.04 (cited in S12 discussion).

safety_signals.quote: Overall, 34.2% of patients who received extended-release niacin and 32.5% of patients who received placebo had serious adverse events during follow-up (P = 0.30).
safety_signals.note: Registry S2 SAE counts 587/1718 vs 551/1696 match.
Registry table values (no prose quote): 45 vs 38, HR 1.17 (0.76-1.80), p=0.47.

genetics.finding: Heterozygous ABCA1 loss-of-function mutations lower HDL-C by 17 mg/dL without increasing ischemic heart disease risk
genetics.effect: HR 0.67 (0.28-1.61) in CCHS; null in two other Copenhagen studies
genetics.quote: Heterozygotes vs noncarriers for 4 ABCA1 mutations (P1065S, G1216V, N1800H, R2144X) had HDL cholesterol levels of 41 mg/dL (interquartile range, 31-50 mg/dL) vs 58 mg/dL (interquartile range, 46-73 mg/dL), corresponding to a reduction in HDL cholesterol of 17 mg/dL (P < .001).
genetics.note: PRE-readout (2008). Abstract read; Europe PMC date 2008-06-01 (JAMA issue 4 June 2008).

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: HDL-raising LIPG Asn396Ser and a 14-SNP HDL score not associated with MI risk (LDL score strongly associated)
genetics.effect: LIPG OR 0.99 (0.88-1.11); HDL score OR 0.93 (0.68-1.26) per 1 SD; LDL score OR 2.13 (1.69-2.69) per 1 SD
genetics.quote: However, a 1 SD increase in HDL cholesterol due to genetic score was not associated with risk of myocardial infarction (OR 0·93, 95% CI 0·68–1·26, p=0·63).
genetics.note: POST AIM-HIGH readout (2011-05-26) — not available before readout.

genetics.finding: LPA variants raising Lp(a) are strongly associated with coronary disease, supporting causal Lp(a)
genetics.effect: OR 1.51 (one variant) and 2.57 (two or more) for CAD with LPA genotype score
genetics.quote: Our findings provide support for a causal role of Lp(a) lipoprotein in coronary disease.
genetics.note: PRE-readout. Relevant because niacin lowers Lp(a) ~19% placebo-adjusted in AIM-HIGH.

genetics.finding: Mouse knockout: PUMA-G (Hcar2) required for niacin anti-lipolytic and acute FFA/TG lowering
genetics.quote: In mice lacking PUMA-G, the nicotinic acid-induced decrease in free fatty acid (FFA) and triglyceride plasma levels was abrogated, indicating that PUMA-G mediates the anti-lipolytic and lipid-lowering effects of nicotinic acid in vivo.
genetics.note: Animal evidence only. Human genetic evidence on HCAR2 and CVD: NOT FOUND.

genetics.finding: GPR109A-knockout mice retain niacin lipid efficacy; full GPR109A agonists (MK-1903, SCH900271) did not reproduce niacin lipid effects in humans
genetics.effect: Target (HCAR2) does not mediate lipid efficacy
genetics.quote: In mice, the absence of GPR109A had no effect on niacin's lipid efficacy despite complete abrogation of the anti-lipolytic effect.
genetics.note: POST AIM-HIGH readout. Europe PMC lists 2012-08-01; online publication 22 Aug 2012 (issue date not independently verified).

consensus_explanation.summary: The accepted explanation is that the biological hypothesis was wrong or too weak: raising HDL-C (niacin's headline effect) does not causally lower cardiovascular risk (later supported by Mendelian randomization and the CETP-inhibitor trials), and niacin's potentially useful apoB/LDL-C and Lp(a) reductions were small on top of an intensive statin (+/- ezetimibe) background in which LDL-C was already ~71 mg/dL. Between-arm differences were only ~5 mg/dL LDL-C and ~5 mg/dL HDL-C (~11% apoB), which by CTT-type estimates predicts <10% relative risk reduction, far below the 25% the trial was powered for. Design features amplified the null: both arms were titrated to the same LDL-C target (more statin/ezetimibe in the placebo arm), placebo tablets contained 50 mg IR niacin, the endpoint was expanded mid-trial because events were too few, and the trial (~3,400 patients, 556 events) was stopped early for futility, so it could not exclude a modest benefit. An unexplained ischemic stroke excess and (later) serious infection/GI excess added harm signals. HPS2-THRIVE subsequently confirmed no benefit with excess harm.

pre_readout.note: Readout = NHLBI announcement 2011-05-26. Sources with pub_date before that date counted as available.
available_before_readout: Design: N≈3,300-3,414, 850 planned events, 85% power for 25% RRR, LDL-C 40-80 mg/dL target in both arms, endpoint expansion (S3, S4; 2011-02-02); registry since 2005-07-15 (S2).
Baseline: mean LDL-C 71 mg/dL, HDL-C 34.9 mg/dL, median TG 161 mg/dL among statin users (S4; 2011-02-02).
Coronary Drug Project: niacin reduced nonfatal MI ~24%/stroke ~22% (as summarized in S3) in pre-statin era (S13; 1975); 15-year mortality 52.0% vs 58.2% (S14; 1986).
HATS: simvastatin+niacin LDL -42%, HDL +26%, clinical events 3% vs 24% placebo in 160 patients (S15; 2001).
ARBITER 2: ER niacin 1000 mg on statin, HDL-C +21%, CIMT progression difference P=0.08 (S16; 2004).
ARBITER 6-HALTS: ER niacin vs ezetimibe on statin, HDL-C +18.4%, CIMT regression favoring niacin (S17; 2009).
Bruckert meta-analysis of 11 niacin RCTs (mostly pre-statin): major coronary events -25%, any CV event -27% (S18; 2009).
SEACOAST II: niacin ER/simvastatin 2000/40 vs simvastatin 80: HDL-C +21.9%, TG -31.8%, Lp(a) -21.0% (S19; 2008).
Genetics: ABCA1 LoF lowers HDL-C without raising IHD risk (S20; 2008); LPA variants support causal Lp(a) (S24; 2009).
CTT 2010: ~22% RR reduction per 1 mmol/L LDL-C lowering, including at LDL-C <2 mmol/L (S25; 2010-11-08) — implies small expected benefit from ~0.12 mmol/L LDL difference.
Target biology: HCAR2 (PUMA-G/HM74) mediates anti-lipolysis in mice (S22; 2003).
only_after_readout: Full results incl. HR 1.02 (0.87-1.21), lipid changes (S1 NEJM, 2011-11-15).
Lauring 2012: niacin lipid efficacy independent of GPR109A (S23; 2012-08).
Final ischemic stroke analysis (S8; 2013) and serious adverse event profile incl. infection excess (S9; 2014).

access_summary.note: Key numbers = design (n, follow-up, planned events, RRR, power, alpha), outcome (HR, CI low/high, p, events x2), placebo-adjusted biomarkers (HDL-C, LDL-C, TG, apoB, apoA-1, Lp(a), non-HDL-C). Each assigned to most accessible category. Open: n (also in S3 flow), planned events, RRR, power, alpha, HDL-C abs, LDL-C abs, apoB, apoA-1, Lp(a). Registry: follow-up, HR, CI low, CI high, events x2. Abstract only: p=0.79 (registry gives 0.80, different test). Paywalled only: placebo-adjusted TG % (only in NEJM full text; available free solely via secondary blog). Not found: non-HDL-C. NEJM full text (S1) returned HTTP 403 and is not in PMC.

open_questions: AIM-HIGH NEJM full text (S1) could not be accessed (HTTP 403; not in PMC). Placebo-adjusted percent changes for HDL-C and TG come only from the NEJM CardioExchange blog summary (S10); placebo-adjusted LDL-C/HDL-C absolute differences come from HPS2-THRIVE papers citing AIM-HIGH (S11: 0.12/0.13 mmol/L; S12: 5/5 mg/dL).
p-value: NEJM abstract P=0.79 (log-rank) vs registry p=0.80 (Cox adjusted for gender and diabetes).
Follow-up: NHLBI at stopping said actual average 32 months (S5); NEJM/registry report mean 36 months (includes close-out). Median follow-up NOT FOUND.
Ischemic stroke counts differ across stages: interim press coverage 28 vs 12 (secondary, not verified), NEJM first-event 1.6% vs 0.9% (via S10), final adjudicated 32 vs 18, HR 1.78 (S8).
Number of primary events at the DSMB interim look (25 April 2011) NOT FOUND; fraction of planned events (0.65) computed from final counts 556/850.
Alpha for the amended 850-event design is not explicitly stated; 0.025 one-sided is from the original design statement (S3).
LDL-C assay method (Friedewald vs direct) NOT FOUND; core lab was Northwest Lipid Metabolism and Diabetes Research Laboratories.
apoB/Lp(a) effects (S7) are restricted to prior-statin users with paired baseline/1-year samples (~2,867 of 3,414).
Design paper statement on statin-trial risk reduction differs trivially between abstract ('25%-35%') and body text ('25–40%') of S3.
